bib.title: Chapter 1. Why Reinforcement Learning? (Reinforcement Learning: Industrial Applications of Intelligent Agents)

question: Why do engineers need reinforcement learning, when is it the right tool, and what are its basic ideas and history?
contributions: Informal introduction to RL: four components (agent, environment, action, reward), when to use RL, industry applications, a taxonomy of algorithm families, a first value-estimation model (Rescorla-Wagner) and a short history.

limits: Introductory and informal; no experiments, hyperparameters or benchmarks.
Author states he simplified the mathematics and dropped formal notation.
Written 2020: predates RLHF and LLM applications; says nothing about language models.
Data figures are secondary citations (IDC, Gartner).
Equations 1-1 to 1-3 and the vectors did not survive text extraction.
practices: Choose the simplest solution that solves the problem to a satisfactory level (TIP, When Should You Use RL?).
Use RL when decisions are sequential and actions lead to exploration; avoid forcing RL onto prediction tasks such as stock prediction (When Should You Use RL?).
Keep the reward as simple as you can; use the natural reward where one exists (Reinforcement Learning).
Prefer supervised learning when ground truth can be obtained, since without it performance is hard to quantify (Machine Learning).
Use reward shaping (reward engineering) to give more frequent feedback under delayed rewards (Delayed rewards).
Update weights gradually with a step size between zero and one rather than jumping to the answer, since outcomes are noisy (Weight update rule).
Prefer model-free algorithms for general industrial problems; use bespoke model-based RL when the environment has strict static rules (Model-Free or Model-Based).
Consider the ethics and risks of what you build (RL Applications).

terms.definition: RL tells you how to make the best decisions, sequentially, within a context, to maximize a real-life measure of success.
Accepts actions and responds with the result and a new set of observations.
Feedback telling the agent which actions led to success or failure; typically numeric but only needs to reinforce behavior.
The correct term for the agent's strategy; the strategy that maximizes reward.
terms.where: How Agents Use and Update Their Strategy

terms.definition: Model-based algorithms use definitive knowledge of the environment; model-free learn strategies through interaction.
Online agents improve using only data just observed and discard it; offline agents learn from offline datasets or old logs.
terms.where: How Agents Use and Update Their Strategy

terms.definition: On-policy agents predict reward after choosing actions per the current strategy; off-policy agents predict reward after choosing any action.
terms.where: How Agents Use and Update Their Strategy

terms.definition: Value-based: try actions, record results, follow the strategy that gave the best result. Policy-based: tweak model parameters toward actions that produced the best result.
Prediction predicts a numerical outcome from observations (regression); control adds the freedom to choose actions.
terms.where: Is RL the Same as ML?

terms.definition: Altering the reward signal so it provides more frequent updates; also called reward engineering.
Actor makes decisions to maximize reward; critic plans ahead and corrects the actor.
Difference between the actual outcome and the value estimate; a form of surprise.
